terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō), deponent; future participle moritūrus
evidence: Cic. Sen. 74: moriendum enim certē est
terms.comment: What one dies of goes in the ablative: famē morī, to die of hunger (Cic. Att. 6.1.6, Lewis & Short). Plants die too: a bush sī exāruit, moritur, if it dries out, dies (Varr. LL 5.102). Moriar, sī …, may I die if … (Cic. Att. 8.6.4).

evidence: Phaedr. 3.16.19: sīc vīva quod negārat tribuit mortua

terms.comment: The gentle word of letters; in full dē vītā dēcēdere (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.21.1: omnium rērum mors est extrēmum (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: bubble out one’s soul: kick the bucket
terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Petr.; Sen. Apoc.
evidence: Petr. 42.3; 62.10; Sen. Apoc. 4.2 (Lewis & Short), s.v. ēbulliō
terms.comment: Traupman prints animam bullīre; the phrase Lewis & Short cites from Petronius and Seneca is with ēbullīre.

phrases.latin: passer mortuus est meae puellae, passer, dēliciae meae puellae
phrases.english: my girl’s sparrow is dead, the sparrow, my girl’s pet

phrases.latin: Moriendum enim certē est, et incertum an hōc ipsō diē.
phrases.english: For die we certainly must, and no one knows whether it will be this very day.

sources: Lewis & Short: morior · Lewis & Short: mortuus · Lewis & Short: decedo · Lewis & Short: anima · Lewis & Short: mors
